lessons.title: The Dignity of Human Life and Religious Freedom

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which religious believers promote human dignity in practice.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: charitable giving (tzedakah, zakat, sewa, dana) / campaigning for human rights / providing humanitarian aid through faith charities / conscientious objection / community service. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What does Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protect?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for: freedom of religion or belief, including the freedom to change religion and to express it in worship, teaching, practice, and observance [1 mark for identifying freedom of religion; 2 marks for adding the right to change religion and/or express it publicly]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the concept of imago Dei shapes Christian teaching on human rights.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed description of imago Dei (Genesis 1:26-27 — created in God's image), how it gives every person inherent dignity regardless of background, the Catholic Catechism's development (1929-1933: social justice; 1905-1912: common good), and how this motivates agape in action — charity, advocacy, conscientious objection.
Secure: Two or more elements described with explanation of why imago Dei matters.
Developing: Basic description of imago Dei with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement that Christians believe in human dignity. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious teachings that emphasise the value and dignity of every human life.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct teachings from different traditions, each with a named source and interpretation. E.g. Genesis 1:26-27 (imago Dei — made in God's image so every life is sacred); Qur'an 5:32 (saving one life is like saving all of humanity — grounds Islamic human rights ethics); Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (saving one life saves an entire world — underpins Jewish tzedakah). Each developed with explanation.
Secure: Two teachings with named sources; adequate explanation.
Developing: Two teachings; one developed.
Emerging: One teaching, limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting views on whether religious believers should follow the law of the land when it conflicts with their faith.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: View 1 — religious conviction may require civil disobedience when law is unjust (Martin Luther King's Letter from Birmingham Jail; the tradition of conscientious objection; prophetic tradition of challenging unjust laws). View 2 — most religious traditions teach respect for civil authority (Romans 13:1 for Christians; Islamic principle of following legitimate authority; Sikh legal cases resolved through courts rather than disobedience). Both views developed with named sources.
Secure: Two contrasting views each with a source; clear explanation.
Developing: Two views; limited source use.
Emerging: One view described. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious freedom should never be restricted by the laws of a country.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to religious teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Article 18 UDHR protects religious freedom as a fundamental right; all traditions affirm the right to practise faith; Sikhs won legal cases to wear religious items; persecution of religious minorities shows the harm caused when states suppress faith; Humanists also support Article 18 as a universal right.
Arguments against: Religious freedom can conflict with others' rights (e.g. a registrar refusing same-sex ceremonies); religious extremism shows that unlimited religious freedom can enable harm; courts have legitimately limited religious expression that incites hatred; the common good (Catholic concept, Catechism 1905-1912) sometimes requires individual freedoms to be balanced against community welfare.
Conclusion: Most traditions accept some limits on freedom when it harms others, but the default should be maximum freedom. Humanists and most religious traditions agree that no one should face persecution for their beliefs.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources including Article 18 UDHR, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 5 SPaG]

before.content_html:
Prejudice, Discrimination, and the Law

Prejudice is an unfair, preconceived attitude towards a person or group. Discrimination is when that prejudice is acted upon — treating people unequally or unjustly. The UK Equality Act 2010 makes it illegal to discriminate on the grounds of nine “protected characteristics,” including race and religion. Despite legal protections, racial prejudice and discrimination remain significant social problems that religious communities have addressed both theologically and practically.

Christianity: All Made in God’s Image

Christian teaching grounds racial equality in the doctrine of imago Dei — every person is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27) — and in the teaching of Jesus. Galatians 3:27–29 declares that in Christ “there is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Acts 10:34–35 records Peter’s declaration that “God does not show favouritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him and does what is right.” These passages have historically been used to argue that racial discrimination is incompatible with Christian faith.

The Catholic Catechism paragraphs 1934–1938 explicitly address social equality, stating that every form of social or cultural discrimination in fundamental personal rights on the grounds of race is contrary to God’s design. The Catechism teaches that differences between persons belong to God’s plan and that solidarity requires recognising these differences while treating all people as equal in dignity.

Key Fact

Acts 10:34–35 records Peter declaring that “God does not show favouritism but accepts from every nation the one who fears him.” Catholic Catechism 1934–1938 states that racial discrimination in fundamental personal rights is contrary to God’s design.

Martin Luther King and Christian Activism

Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist minister who led the American Civil Rights Movement and drew explicitly on Christian theology to oppose racial discrimination. In his “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963), written while imprisoned for civil disobedience, King argued that unjust laws — laws that degrade human personality and contradict natural and divine law — need not be obeyed. He cited Augustine and Aquinas in support of the distinction between just and unjust laws.

King’s theology was rooted in agape — unconditional love for all people including one’s opponents — and in the Christian vision of the “beloved community” where all people are treated as equally beloved children of God. His work illustrates how Christian teaching on racial equality can motivate non-violent direct action.

Judaism: Every Person Is a World

Jewish teaching grounds racial equality in b’tselem Elohim — every person is made in the image of God — and in the Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, which states that God created the first human as a single individual so that no one could say “my ancestor is greater than yours.” This passage explicitly argues against racial and ethnic hierarchy.

Jewish organisations have historically worked against racial discrimination. HIAS (the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society), founded in 1881, provides humanitarian aid and legal assistance to refugees and migrants regardless of religion or background, arguing that Jewish memory of persecution and displacement creates a moral obligation to protect the vulnerable. Jewish teaching on tikkun olam — repairing the world — motivates social justice work including anti-racism campaigns.

Islam: No Arab Is Superior to a Non-Arab

Islamic teaching strongly opposes racial discrimination. Qur’an 49:13 states that God created human beings from a single pair of a male and female and made them into different nations and tribes “so that you may know one another” — diversity is presented as God’s design, not a basis for hierarchy. Qur’an 5:8 commands believers to be “persistently standing firm in justice” and not to allow hatred of a people to cause them to act unjustly.

The Prophet Muhammad’s farewell sermon, as transmitted in Islamic tradition, is reported to have declared that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, and no non-Arab is superior to an Arab; no white person is superior to a black person, and no black person to a white, except through piety and good deeds. The ummah is explicitly a global community transcending racial boundaries. British organisations such as the Christian Muslim Forum work to build understanding between Christian and Muslim communities and to tackle prejudice and discrimination together.

Hindu teaching on human equality faces a particular historical challenge: the varna system (sometimes confused with caste) has been used to justify social stratification. The Rig Veda 10:90 (the Purusha Sukta) describes the four varnas as emerging from the body of the cosmic person, which some have read as a divinely ordained hierarchy.

However, reformers have strongly challenged discrimination based on birth. Mahatma Gandhi campaigned against the treatment of “Harijans” (his term for Dalits) as untouchables, arguing this was contrary to the Hindu principle of universal brotherhood. Dr B.R. Ambedkar (1891–1956), himself a Dalit, was more critical of Hinduism’s caste structures. He eventually converted to Buddhism in 1956, arguing that Buddhism’s rejection of caste offered genuine equality. Reform movements including Vivekananda’s Ramakrishna Mission and ISKCON (the International Society for Krishna Consciousness) have emphasised the universal presence of Brahman in all people regardless of birth, challenging caste-based discrimination.

Sikhism: The Khalsa and Equality

Sikhism teaches the fundamental equality of all people before God. The Guru Granth Sahib at ang 349 contains teachings emphasising that God created all humanity from the same divine light and that there is no high or low in God’s creation. Guru Gobind Singh’s founding of the Khalsa in 1699 was explicitly about dismantling social hierarchies: initiates from all castes drank from the same bowl, symbolising equality. The Khalsa’s stated purpose included protecting the oppressed and challenging tyranny.

In contemporary Britain, Sikh organisations have worked against racism. Khalsa Aid not only provides humanitarian relief but also advocates for human rights. The gurdwara’s langar (community kitchen), which is open to all regardless of background, is a practical daily expression of the principle that no one is superior to another in God’s eyes.

Buddhism: Right Action and the Rejection of Hierarchy

The Buddhist concept of Right Action — part of the Noble Eightfold Path — requires avoiding actions that harm others, including discrimination. Buddhist teaching holds that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and are capable of liberation, making no person inherently superior or inferior to another.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s mass conversion movement brought millions of Dalits to Buddhism in 1956 as a means of escaping caste-based discrimination. He argued that the Buddha had taught the equality of all people regardless of birth — a radical claim in the context of mid-twentieth century India. However, the spec also notes that some Buddhist monks in Myanmar have been associated with the 969 Movement, which has at times promoted anti-Muslim sentiment — a controversial example of how religious identity can also become entangled with ethnic nationalism rather than transcending it. Scholars and many Buddhist leaders have condemned this as contrary to Buddhist teaching on compassion and non-harm.

Key Fact

Qur’an 49:13 teaches that God made people into different nations and tribes so that they might know one another — diversity as divine design. The Guru Granth Sahib (ang 349) teaches that God created all humanity from the same divine light and that there is no high or low in God’s creation.

Humanists UK holds that racial discrimination is irrational and harmful, and that every person deserves equal respect on the basis of their humanity, not because of any religious teaching. Amnesty International — which includes many secular and non-religious supporters — campaigns globally against racial discrimination, arbitrary detention, and the treatment of minorities. Humanists argue that the moral case against racism does not require religious grounding: reason and empathy are sufficient to recognise that all people share the same capacity to suffer, flourish, and pursue a meaningful life.

practice_questions.text:
'Religion is the most important reason why people work against racial discrimination.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to religious teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Martin Luther King grounded civil rights work explicitly in Christian agape and the beloved community; Islamic ummah transcends racial boundaries (Qur'an 49:13); Sikh Khalsa was founded partly to protect the oppressed; Jewish tikkun olam and HIAS work motivated by religious memory of persecution; Gandhi and Ambedkar both drew on religious frameworks.
Arguments against: Amnesty International and Humanists UK work against racism without religious grounding, using reason and empathy; secular laws (UK Equality Act 2010) provide legal protection regardless of religion; some discrimination has been committed by religious groups (caste in Hinduism, 969 Movement); science and human rights law offer non-religious arguments for equality.
Conclusion: Religion has been enormously important historically but is not the only motivation; a justified conclusion should weigh both religious and secular sources.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 5 SPaG]

lessons.title: Wealth, Poverty and the Work of Faith Charities

before.content_html:
Wealth, Poverty, and Religious Ethics

Religious traditions do not uniformly condemn wealth, but they do consistently place ethical demands on how it is acquired and used. Two forms of poverty frame the issue. Absolute poverty is the state of lacking basic necessities for survival. Relative poverty is being significantly worse off than others in the same society. Both forms exist in Britain and globally. Religious traditions draw on scripture and teaching to explain why poverty matters morally and how believers should respond through individual action and institutional charity.

Christianity: Wealth as Stewardship

Christianity teaches that wealth is not wrong in itself, but its acquisition and use carry moral weight. Several Gospel parables directly address wealth. Luke 16:19–31, the parable of the rich man (Dives) and Lazarus, describes a wealthy man who ignores a poor man at his gate; after death their situations are dramatically reversed. The parable implies that ignoring the poor has eternal consequences.

Luke 12:13–21, the parable of the rich fool, criticises a man who builds larger barns to store surplus grain and says to himself “You have plenty of good things laid up for many years. Take life easy; eat, drink and be merry” — only to die that very night. The parable warns against treating wealth as the ultimate security. Mark 10:21–31 records Jesus telling a rich young man to sell everything, give to the poor, and follow him. Mark 12:41–44, the story of the widow’s offering, praises a poor widow who gives two small coins, more than the wealthy who give from their surplus. These passages together suggest that what matters is not the amount given but the sacrifice and the spirit behind the giving.

Christian Aid and CAFOD (the Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) are major British faith charities that apply these teachings internationally. Christian Aid works across more than 50 countries, campaigning against the causes of poverty as well as providing emergency relief. CAFOD, the official Catholic development agency for England and Wales, works in partnership with local organisations worldwide, motivated by Catholic social teaching on solidarity and the preferential option for the poor. The Trussell Trust, which operates a network of food banks across Britain, was founded as a Christian charity.

Key Fact

Key Gospel passages on wealth: Luke 16:19–31 (rich man and Lazarus — ignoring poverty has eternal consequences), Luke 12:13–21 (rich fool — wealth is not ultimate security), Mark 10:21–31 (sell everything and give to the poor), Mark 12:41–44 (widow’s mite — sacrifice matters more than amount).

Judaism: Tzedakah and the Eight Levels of Giving

Tzedakah — charitable giving — is a core Jewish obligation, not merely an optional act of kindness. It is rooted in the understanding that wealth ultimately belongs to God and that sharing it is an act of justice. The twelfth-century philosopher Maimonides described eight levels of tzedakah, from the lowest (giving reluctantly and inadequately) to the highest (helping someone become financially self-sufficient, thereby removing their need for charity altogether).

World Jewish Relief is the primary British Jewish charity working to alleviate poverty, operating in Eastern Europe and other regions affected by poverty and conflict. HIAS supports refugees globally. These organisations embody tzedakah in action, working on the principle that Jewish memory of persecution creates a specific obligation to protect the vulnerable. Concern for the ger (the stranger) is also a repeated Torah commandment, grounding Jewish poverty relief in theological duty.

Islam: Zakat and the Purification of Wealth

Islam’s approach to wealth includes both a theological and a practical dimension. Qur’an 2:177 describes true righteousness as including giving wealth to those in need: to relatives, orphans, the needy, travellers, those who ask, and for the freeing of captives. This is not voluntary generosity — it describes the character of a truly righteous person.

Zakat is the third Pillar of Islam: every Muslim who holds wealth above a minimum threshold (nisab) for a full lunar year must give 2.5% to those in need. Zakat is not charity but a religious obligation — it purifies the rest of one’s wealth by acknowledging that a portion belongs to the poor. Islamic Relief and Muslim Aid are major British Islamic charities that channel zakat and voluntary donations to emergency relief and long-term development projects worldwide, working in conflict zones and areas of extreme poverty.

Hinduism’s approach to wealth is shaped by the concept of artha — the legitimate pursuit of wealth and worldly success, one of the four aims of human life (purusharthas). Unlike some traditions that view wealth with suspicion, Hinduism acknowledges artha as a proper human goal, provided it is pursued within the constraints of dharma (righteousness). Wealth acquired unethically or used selfishly, however, generates negative karma.

Dana — charitable giving — is a virtuous act in Hinduism, generating good karma and expressing the understanding that the divine is present in every person. Food for Life Global, founded within the Vaishnava (ISKCON) tradition, provides free vegetarian meals to people in need worldwide, making it one of the world’s largest food relief programmes. It operates on the principle that food is spiritual and sharing it with all people is an act of worship.

Sikhism: Sewa and Langar

Sikh teaching presents wealth as a trust from God. The Guru Granth Sahib at ang 1246 contains teachings on the duty of giving to those in need. Sewa — selfless service — is one of the three pillars of Sikhism (alongside naam japna and kirat karo). Giving generously and without discrimination is expected of all Sikhs. The langar — the free community kitchen in every gurdwara — is a daily, practical expression of sewa: anyone, regardless of wealth, religion, or status, is welcome to eat there at no cost.

Khalsa Aid is a British Sikh humanitarian organisation that provides emergency food, water, and shelter in disaster zones and conflict areas worldwide, explicitly motivated by the Sikh teaching of sewa and the principle that every human being deserves dignity. The Guru Granth Sahib at ang 42 also contains teachings linking righteous giving to spiritual advancement.

Buddhism: The Middle Way and Right Livelihood

Buddhism’s approach to wealth is shaped by the story of Siddhartha Gautama himself. Born into wealth, he abandoned it; after extreme asceticism failed him, he found the Middle Way — neither excessive wealth nor extreme poverty. The Four Noble Truths identify tanha (craving or attachment) as the root of suffering. Attachment to wealth — treating it as a source of lasting happiness — leads to dukkha.

Right Livelihood — the fifth step of the Eightfold Path — requires earning a living in ways that do not cause harm. Dana (generosity and charitable giving) is one of the ten Buddhist perfections (paramis) and the first step on the path. Triratna Buddhists in Britain practise dana in their communities. Karuna Trust is a British Buddhist charity that works to relieve poverty and social exclusion, particularly among Dalit communities in South Asia — addressing both material poverty and the structural discrimination that causes it.

Key Fact

Key faith charities: CAFOD and Christian Aid (Christian — overseas development and emergency relief), World Jewish Relief (Jewish — Eastern Europe and conflict regions), Islamic Relief and Muslim Aid (Islamic — disaster zones globally), Khalsa Aid (Sikh — humanitarian relief worldwide), Karuna Trust (Buddhist — Dalit communities, South Asia), Food for Life (Hindu/ISKCON — global food relief).

Humanists UK and secular organisations argue that poverty should be addressed on the basis of rational ethics and compassion, without the need for religious motivation. The utilitarian argument — associated with philosophers like Peter Singer — holds that if we can prevent suffering at relatively little cost to ourselves, we have a moral obligation to do so. Singer has argued that wealthy individuals in developed nations are morally obligated to give significantly more to effective anti-poverty organisations than most currently do. Secular organisations such as Oxfam and Shelter work alongside faith charities to address poverty, driven by a shared moral commitment to human wellbeing regardless of theological grounding.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious people have a greater duty than non-religious people to help those living in poverty.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to religious teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Zakat is a religious obligation — Muslims are commanded to give regardless of personal desire; Christian Aid and CAFOD are motivated by specific theological imperatives (Luke 16:19-31; Catholic preferential option for the poor); tzedakah is a Jewish justice-obligation; sewa is a Sikh pillar of practice, not optional; these traditions make helping the poor a divine command rather than personal choice.
Arguments against: Humanist and secular arguments (e.g. Peter Singer's utilitarian case) impose equal or greater duty based on reason alone; Oxfam and Shelter work alongside faith charities without religious motivation; the UK's welfare state redistributes wealth through taxation regardless of religion; a wealthy non-religious person who gives generously may fulfil a greater practical duty than a religious person who gives little.
Conclusion: should consider whether the source of obligation (divine command vs rational ethics) makes a genuine difference to the duty itself, and reach a clear personal stance.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources including charities and scripture, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 5 SPaG]

lessons.title: Evaluating Human Rights and Final Exam Skills

before.content_html:
Human Rights: The Big Picture

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), adopted by the United Nations in 1948, established a global framework of rights to which every person is entitled regardless of nationality, faith or background. Article 18 of the UDHR guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion — including the freedom to change one’s religion and to manifest it in worship, observance, practice and teaching. This article is particularly important for religious studies because it sits at the intersection of rights and religion: it protects religious believers but also protects those who reject religion.

In this final lesson of the theme we bring together everything you have studied — religious and non-religious perspectives on human dignity, prejudice, discrimination and wealth — and focus on one specific skill: constructing the evaluated, balanced argument that your paper rewards most heavily.

Religious Views on Human Rights and Dignity

Each of the traditions you have studied grounds human rights in a different way, but all affirm the fundamental dignity of every person:

Christianity: Genesis 1:26–27 teaches that every person is made in the image of God (imago Dei). Christians express this in action through agapé — unconditional love in service of others. Christian Aid and church food banks are cited in the spec as examples of this in action. Martin Luther King Jr taught that racial prejudice contradicted the Christian teaching that all people are equal before God.

Judaism: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that every human soul is like a whole world — to save one is to save all, to destroy one is to destroy all. The principle of tzedakah (righteousness/justice) drives Jewish charitable action. On racial prejudice, Jewish charities such as HIAS (Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society) work with refugees worldwide. Maimonides’ Eight Levels of Charity provide a framework for how giving should be practised, with anonymous giving that preserves the recipient’s dignity at the highest levels.

Islam: The Qur’an (5:32) teaches the sacred value of every human life. Ummah — the worldwide community of Muslims — creates an obligation to support all members, regardless of nationality. The Qur’an (49:13) teaches that God created humanity in different nations and tribes so that they may know one another, and that the most honoured person is the most righteous — not the person of the ‘right’ ethnicity or nationality. Islamic Relief operates globally as an expression of this.

Hinduism: The relationship between Brahman (the ultimate reality underlying all existence) and atman (the individual soul) means that the same divine essence is present in every person. This grounds an understanding of human equality that, in theory, transcends caste. Mahatma Gandhi taught that caste discrimination (particularly towards Dalits) contradicted the unity of Brahman that all people share. Hindu charities such as Food for Life provide vegetarian meals globally as an expression of dharma in action.

Sikhism: The Guru Granth Sahib (verse 1) opens with the Mool Mantar, which declares God as one, without hate, without fear — and the consequence for human beings is that all are equal before God. Guru Gobind Singh’s formation of the Khalsa emphasised equality across caste and social boundaries. The Sikh principle of seva (selfless service) drives charities such as Khalsa Aid, which provides disaster relief worldwide without discrimination.

Buddhism: The five Precepts and the Noble Eightfold Path together promote right action and the avoidance of harm. The concept of dhamma in action means living the Buddha’s teachings in service of others. Dr Ambedkar, who led the mass conversion of Dalits to Buddhism in 1956, used Buddhist egalitarianism as the basis for challenging caste discrimination. The Karuna Trust supports the most marginalised in society as an expression of Buddhist compassion (karuṇā).

Non-Religious Views on Human Rights

Humanist UK takes a secular approach to human rights, grounding them in human reason and empathy rather than divine command. Humanists argue that rights do not depend on God — they are justified by our shared capacity for suffering and flourishing. Amnesty International campaigns for human rights from a non-religious standpoint, focusing on freedom from torture, political imprisonment, and the death penalty. Article 18 UDHR (freedom of religion or belief) is important to both organisations: they defend religious believers’ rights even while arguing that law and public policy should be made on secular grounds.

The Humanist view is that rights are grounded in a situationist or relativist framework — what matters is the impact on actual people in actual circumstances, not adherence to a doctrinal rule derived from scripture. This contrasts with religious ‘absolutist’ approaches (particularly in Catholic natural law or Islamic divine command) that hold certain acts to be always and everywhere wrong regardless of consequences.

Key Fact

Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including the right to change religion. The two named non-religious organisations in this theme are Humanist UK (formerly British Humanist Association) and Amnesty International.

Constructing the 15-Mark Evaluation Answer

The 15-mark evaluation question is worth more than any other question type in your paper. Examiners report that most mark loss happens here, and that the most common failures are: giving only one side; using bullet points (which prevent the evaluative language needed for higher marks); and failing to reach a clear, justified conclusion.

Stage 1 — Agree: Write a paragraph arguing in favour of the statement. Use at least one named religious source of authority (scripture, a named scholar or a named religious document). Explain what the source says and why it supports the statement. Connect the source to the specific claim in the question.

Stage 2 — Disagree: Write a paragraph arguing against the statement. Use a contrasting source — either a different religious tradition or a non-religious perspective. Humanist UK, Amnesty International, and non-religious arguments (autonomy, quality of life, situationist ethics) are all valid here. Do not simply copy Stage 1 and add ‘not’. The opposing argument needs its own logic.

Stage 3 — Weighing: Write a sentence or short paragraph that weighs the two sides against each other. Language like ‘However, critics of this view argue…’, ‘This position is compelling because… but it fails to account for…’ or ‘Both sides agree that… but they differ on…’ signals to the examiner that you are evaluating, not merely describing.

Stage 4 — Conclusion: State your personal view clearly. ‘On balance, I agree/disagree because…’ You must justify your conclusion by referring back to the argument. An unjustified conclusion (‘I think everyone has rights’) will not score Mastering.

Key Fact

A Mastering evaluation answer has: an agree paragraph with a named religious source and explanation, a disagree paragraph with a contrasting source (including a non-religious view), evaluative language that weighs the two sides, and a clear justified conclusion. Written in continuous prose — never bullet points.

Timing, SPaG and Final Exam Strategy

Your paper includes spelling, punctuation and grammar (SPaG) marks attached to the 15-mark evaluation question. This means accurate writing is assessed directly. Use full sentences. Check that each sentence ends with a full stop. Capital letters for proper nouns (God, Torah, Qur’an, Buddha). Be consistent with religious terms — decide before the exam whether you will use ‘Qur’an’ or ‘Quran’ and stick to it.

Manage your time carefully. The 15-mark question should receive the most time — aim for at least twelve minutes. Shorter questions (2 marks) should take no more than two minutes. Read the question carefully: ‘explain two beliefs’ requires two developed beliefs with sources, not four brief points. ‘Describe’ asks for recall with meaning; ‘explain’ asks for the religious significance behind a practice or belief.

A common error is to write at length on 5-mark questions and then run out of time for the 15-mark question. The marks per minute return is much higher on the 15-mark question — give it the time it deserves. If you run short, write your conclusion first before filling in the body of the argument — an answer with a conclusion but a thin body will score higher than one with a detailed first paragraph and no conclusion at all.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Article 18 of the UDHR (1948) protects freedom of religion or belief. The named non-religious organisations in this theme are Humanist UK (secular human rights, autonomy-based) and Amnesty International (freedom from torture and political imprisonment). Religious traditions ground human rights in imago Dei (Christianity), tzedakah (Judaism), ummah (Islam), Brahman-atman unity (Hinduism), equality before God / seva (Sikhism), and dhamma in action (Buddhism).
  • The 15-mark evaluation question requires: an agree argument with a named source, a disagree argument with a contrasting source (including a non-religious view), evaluative weighing language, and a clear justified conclusion — all written in continuous prose. SPaG marks apply.
  • Exam strategy: give the 15-mark question at least 12 minutes. If time is short, write your conclusion before completing the body. Never bullet-point your 15-mark answer. ‘Explain two beliefs’ questions require two developed beliefs each with a named source of wisdom or authority.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 15-mark question, the difference between Mastering and Secure often comes down to whether you have included a non-religious view alongside religious ones. Humanist UK and Amnesty International are both named in the spec for this theme — use them. Remember that the 15-mark question carries SPaG marks: accuracy of spelling and grammar is part of your score. Write ‘Qur’an’, ‘Torah’ and ‘Catechism’ with capital letters and correct spelling. Paragraph breaks between ‘agree’, ‘disagree’ and ‘conclusion’ sections make your structure visible to the examiner.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which religious believers act to promote human rights.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each of two correct examples from: Christian Aid / food banks (Christianity) / HIAS or World Jewish Relief (Judaism) / Islamic Relief (Islam) / Food for Life (Hinduism) / Khalsa Aid (Sikhism) / Karuna Trust (Buddhism). Accept other correct examples from the spec. Each must be a religious action, not a general statement.

practice_questions.text: What does Article 18 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protect?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion — including the right to change one's religion and to manifest it in worship, observance, practice and teaching. Secure: Freedom of religion or belief. Developing: Vague — 'the right to have a religion'. Emerging: Incorrect or missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs about the dignity of human life and how these lead to action.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes the Mool Mantar (Guru Granth Sahib 1) on God's nature and its implication that all are equal; the role of seva (selfless service) in Sikh ethics; Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa; Khalsa Aid as a named example of rights-promoting action. Secure: Two or more elements with at least one source. Developing: General statement about Sikh equality without sources. Emerging: Simple mention of Sikhism with no religious grounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Humanist UK's approach to human rights differs from a religious approach.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that Humanist UK grounds rights in reason and shared human capacity for suffering rather than divine command; notes the situationist/relativist approach vs religious absolutism; explains what this means for specific questions (e.g. freedom of religion is valued but religious law should not govern everyone). Secure: Correct contrast between secular and religious grounding with some development. Developing: Vague — 'Humanists don't believe in God' without engaging with the rights argument. Emerging: Confused or incomplete.

practice_questions.text: Explain two religious reasons why racial prejudice and discrimination are wrong.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed reasons from different traditions (e.g. Christian: Martin Luther King / Galatians 3:27-29 — all one in Christ; Islamic: Qur'an 49:13 — God created different peoples to know each other, honour comes from righteousness not race). Each reason explained with a named source and linked explicitly to racial prejudice. Secure: Two reasons with sources; adequate development. Developing: One reason explained; the second underdeveloped. Emerging: General anti-racism statements without religious grounding.

practice_questions.text: 'Religion is the greatest defender of human rights in the modern world.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues for (specific examples of religious charities and activism: Martin Luther King, Khalsa Aid, Islamic Relief, Karuna Trust; religious grounding of dignity in imago Dei, tzedakah, ummah; Article 18 UDHR protects religious freedom). Argues against (religious institutions have also violated rights: historical examples; secular organisations like Amnesty International defend rights independently of religion; Humanist UK argues rights are stronger when grounded in universal reason, not contested doctrine). Weighs both sides. Clear justified personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides with named sources; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided with a brief nod to the other view. Emerging: Simple personal opinion.
